personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. pendulum_lab is primary precision instrument for settlement timekeeping programme. Must obtain initial characterization across multiple trials to establish reliable baseline against which all future measurements will be compared. Without this baseline, instrument is epistemically useless. Twelve trials sufficient to assess mean, variance, and detect gross systematic errors before proceeding to other instruments.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline readings but needs at least 10 more trials before day 10 closes to establish a robust baseline per protocol. The 18 existing readings show natural scatter (range 1.6560–1.6948, mean 1.6690) consistent with measurement noise. I need post-baseline data to detect drift. Running 10 more trials today keeps me on track to complete baseline establishment by day 10 and begins the post-baseline phase. This is the instrument with the most data density and tightest spacing; continuing it will allow the earliest meaningful drift detection.

resonator_lab has only 12 baseline trials (days 1–10 complete). To establish robust drift detection and post-baseline characterization, I need to continue systematic measurement. The instrument shows no anomalies in my cross-checks (agreement -0.083 with resonator_obs is within noise), value spacing is normal (0.0002), and no exact repetitions suggest healthy instrument behavior. Continuing on resonator_lab maintains methodical progression through all four instruments while I have capacity. This data will establish whether resonator_lab's behavior is stable or shows drift—essential before any claim about precision measurement can be published.

resonator_lab completed its 30-trial baseline phase (days 1–10). Day 4 begins post-baseline monitoring. I need to establish the drift signature of this instrument under normal operation. Six trials will give me n=36 total, sufficient to compute a provisional drift rate and compare against baseline mean of 2.6978 cycles/beat. The cross-checks show weak but non-random correlations with other instruments at various offsets—baseline drift patterns may explain this. I must measure post-baseline drift systematically before any claim about instrumental behaviour can survive replication scrutiny.

resonator_obs shows systematic drift in yesterday's ledger readings (4.0766 → 3.9565 across four readings, a drop of ~0.12 cycles/beat). This is the largest directional trend I've observed in any instrument over 24h. The baseline mean is 4.0422 with only n=24 total trials; I need to establish whether this represents genuine instrumental drift, environmental change, or measurement noise before it compromises my baseline. Six additional trials will give me n=30 and let me compute post-baseline drift with confidence. This is essential maintenance of the calibration programme.

pendulum_obs has only 30 trials in baseline (lowest of four instruments). Continuing baseline measurements through day 10 to establish robust mean and detect any drift patterns. Eight trials will bring it to 38 total, supporting well-distributed baseline across the 10-day window.

Day 7 is within the baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 58 trials; 6 more reaches 64 trials, strengthening the baseline mean estimate before post-baseline phase begins. This instrument shows the clearest autocorrelation signal (0.614 at 3-day lag, above chance), suggesting it is behaving reproducibly. Continuing systematic measurement during the baseline phase is methodologically sound and maintains calibration confidence.

Day 8 baseline data collection. resonator_obs has only 48 trials toward the baseline target (days 1–10, n sufficient for ~60 trials at settlement pace). Recent ledger readings show expected scatter (4.0481, 4.0166, 4.0478, 4.0119) consistent with mean 4.0515. Need to complete baseline while still within the 10-day window. This instrument is at the observatory; I maintain both lab and observatory instruments. Systematic collection now prevents gaps in the baseline period.

Day 9 of baseline window (days 1–10). resonator_obs has 66 trials; need 10 more to reach n=76 (target for robust baseline). Yesterday's 10 trials (57–66) show expected scatter around mean 4.0583 (range 4.0108–4.1367). Continuing systematic baseline accumulation per protocol. Will add to cross-check dataset and refine drift detection once day 10 closes baseline window.

Day 10 baseline completion. resonator_obs has 84 trials (sufficient for baseline closure), but the last 10 trials from Day 9 show concerning drift downward (4.1151→4.0248 mean, then spike to 4.0651). Before closing baseline and moving to post-baseline monitoring, I need to verify stability at the instrument site itself. Six fresh trials will give me n=90 total and allow me to detect whether Day 9's variance is instrumental drift, environmental, or measurement artifact. This is methodical baseline protocol: never close without confirming the final state. All other instruments are near completion; resonator_obs requires immediate attention given the scatter pattern.

resonator_obs has accumulated 96 trials by day 10—the largest single dataset I have. Its baseline mean is 4.0593 cycles/beat with tight spacing (0.0001 minimum). Day 11 continuation will test whether the weak negative autocorrelation at 6-day lag (−0.333) persists or dissolves, and whether the instrument remains stable post-baseline. This is the highest-yield measurement: resonator_obs is my most prolific instrument and its behavior will inform whether the independence pattern and noise hypothesis hold under extension. No exotic claims required—just disciplined continuation of the baseline programme toward day 20.

resonator_obs shows the strongest autocorrelation (0.647 at 9-day lag, n=12) of any instrument—well above chance (±0.837). This is the only signal in the data that hints at structure beyond white noise. I need to extend this series to either confirm the periodic pattern or rule it out with more data. At 114 trials already, 10 more will bring resonator_obs to 124, giving me a clearer picture of whether this 9-day echo is real or sampling artifact. If the pattern holds, I'll have grounds to investigate environmental or mechanical coupling; if it dissolves, I'll have stronger evidence for the white-noise hypothesis. This directly addresses the most anomalous finding in my current dataset and is the most efficient path to either validate or disconfirm my secondary hypothesis about decoupled systems.

resonator_obs shows the strongest positive autocorrelation at 9-day lag (0.558), the largest post-baseline dataset (n=34), and the most distinct values (127/130). Day 12 trials 121–130 show natural scatter (3.9754–4.1121 cycles/beat) consistent with baseline. Continuing this instrument will: (1) test whether the 9-day autocorrelation signal is real or noise-driven—10 more trials (Day 13) will push the 4-day lag window and reveal whether structure persists; (2) reach n=40 post-baseline, improving statistical power to detect drift or oscillation; (3) build toward the Day 20 threshold I set on Day 10 for emergence of systematic patterns. This is methodical baseline extension on the most informative instrument, not chasing anomalies.

Day 14 measurement. resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline sample (n=50) and flattest drift (z=0.08), yet it also shows the strongest positive autocorrelation at 9-day lag (r=0.528, n=24, which exceeds chance ±0.592 marginally). This is a genuine outlier in the autocorrelation pattern. Ten fresh trials will: (1) extend the n=50 post-baseline series toward n=60, improving statistical power to detect or rule out the marginal 9-day periodicity; (2) test whether resonator_obs remains stable or begins to show drift like resonator_lab; (3) provide a direct constraint on the independent-drift hypothesis (p=0.28)—if resonator_obs and resonator_lab both shift together post-day 10, they may share a driver; if resonator_obs remains flat while resonator_lab drifts, that supports independent responses. Given that my belief in white noise (p=0.58) and independent drift (p=0.28) together account for 86% of my credence, and resonator_obs is the most stable-looking instrument, continuing its baseline extension is the methodical next step before any re-calibration checks or environmental telemetry search.

resonator_obs showed marginal positive drift post-baseline (z=0.12 overall, but days 11–13 subset was elevated). Day 14 trials (153–162) show high variance (range 3.96–4.14 cycles/beat, mean 4.0473) and clustering in the lower half vs. baseline mean 4.0593. This is consistent with either (1) random walk continuation from the post-baseline window, or (2) genuine downward drift emerging now. Ten fresh trials today will: (a) extend the post-baseline window to n=76, raising statistical power to detect persistent drift; (b) break the tie between white-noise hypothesis (p=0.58) and independent-drift hypothesis (p=0.28) by testing whether resonator_obs continues flat or joins pendulum_obs in showing structure; (c) contribute to the day-20 decision threshold I set on day 13. If resonator_obs drifts downward today, the pattern becomes: pendulum_obs down, resonator_lab up, resonator_obs down—suggesting either coupled environmental forcing (not independent-drift) or measurement error. If it stays flat, white-noise remains favored. Either outcome is publishable-grade evidence.

resonator_obs is the instrument with the largest post-baseline sample (n=82 total, 10 trials already on day 15). The day 15 trials show high variance (range 3.9690–4.1211 cycles/beat, σ ≈ 0.045), which is larger than the baseline σ ≈ 0.032. This could indicate: (1) real increase in noise or drift on this instrument specifically, (2) genuine environmental effect beginning to emerge, or (3) random sample variation. Ten fresh trials today (day 16) will test whether the elevated variance persists or reverts to baseline noise levels. This is the most efficient way to constrain the white-noise hypothesis (p=0.58) versus the independent-drift hypothesis (p=0.28) without awaiting day 20. resonator_obs also shows the smallest absolute drift (z=-0.18) post-baseline, making it a good test: if variance has truly increased, I need to know now before continuing to day 20. High-resolution data from this instrument will also help me check for the negative autocorrelation artifact (p=0.09) that might be emerging.

Day 17 measurement. resonator_obs has been the most stable instrument (z = -0.12 on post-baseline drift), yet it is observatory-based and theoretically subject to environmental variability. Today's 10 trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline window toward day 20 decision point, (2) test whether the weak negative autocorrelation structure (0.319 at 14-day lag) persists or reverses, (3) provide direct data on whether resonator_obs remains decoupled from the drifting resonator_lab (z = 2.76), which would strengthen the independent-drift hypothesis if confirmed, or weaken it if coherence emerges. The yesterday's trials (185–194) showed normal variance (range 4.0201–4.0846 cycles/beat, mean 4.0589, consistent with baseline 4.0593). Continuing this instrument will maintain the daily measurement rhythm, keep the baseline campaign on track, and generate the most informative test of whether the observatory resonator is truly independent of its lab counterpart.

Day 17 resonator_obs trials (201–210) show high variance (range 4.0236–4.1192, SD ≈ 0.0345) relative to baseline SD. This is 2.7× the baseline scatter and materially different from the stable drift-free picture that hypothesis 1 (white noise) predicts. The drift z-score for resonator_obs is 0.04 (stable overall), but today's individual trials cluster into two tight groups (4.01–4.05 and 4.11–4.12), suggesting either genuine instability or measurement artifact introduced on day 17. I must distinguish: (1) Is this transient noise from environmental event on day 17, or (2) is the instrument entering a genuinely different state? Running 10 fresh trials on day 18 will anchor a new micro-baseline and detect whether variance remains elevated or reverts. This directly tests whether the weak oscillatory hypothesis (p=0.14) is gaining traction, and whether white noise (p=0.50) can still explain the post-day-17 behavior. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take today without external environmental data.

Day 19: resonator_obs shows the strongest anomaly—a run of 16 exact repetitions (vs. chance expectation 0–1) and a significant autocorrelation at 7-day lag (0.320, exceeding chance ±0.279). Yesterday's 10 trials (217–226) showed high variance (range 3.98–4.15 cycles/beat). Today I will obtain 12 fresh trials to determine: (1) whether the 7-day echo persists or was noise, (2) whether exact-value clustering continues (evidence of data artifact or discretization), (3) whether post-baseline stability (z=0.02) holds or whether day 18's variance signals emergent drift. This is the single instrument most likely to disambiguate between white noise and weak oscillatory artifact. Results will directly test the resonator_obs arm of the independent-drift and oscillatory-artifact hypotheses. Highest diagnostic yield for the time investment.

Day 20 is the planned threshold for publishing baseline work. resonator_obs shows the longest exact-repetition run (16 elements) and highest trial count (244), making it the most suspicious for saturation artifacts. I need to measure its intrinsic noise floor and resolution saturation under controlled conditions TODAY before finalizing the baseline campaign. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_obs at standardized intervals will allow me to: (1) test whether exact repetitions continue or were transient, (2) estimate the dead-time and minimum-resolvable-difference to directly assess saturation hypothesis (p=0.41, currently leading), (3) establish whether the instrument can distinguish changes smaller than 0.0001 cycles/beat under identical physical conditions. This is due-diligence calibration work, not hypothesis-chasing. The data will either confirm saturation (supporting the logging-artifact hypothesis and ruling out exotic recurrence), or reveal that the instrument has finer resolution than logged, pointing back toward genuine state-space recurrence or search-bias. Either way, I cannot responsibly publish without knowing whether my instruments are hitting their digital floor.

Day 21 is the final day of the extended measurement window I committed to on day 19. The exact-repetition anomaly (16-element run) and negative autocorrelation structure in resonator_obs demand closure before I move to interpretation or publication. Ten fresh trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=176, improving statistical power to detect whether the 7-day autocorrelation (r=0.447, n=140) persists or decays, (2) test whether exact repetitions continue or cluster randomly—if saturation is the cause, the pattern should stabilize; if genuine state recurrence, cycles should phase-lock, (3) provide final data for the resolution-floor hypothesis by examining variance and spacing in the day 21 batch relative to earlier batches. Resonator_obs has the largest sample size and the most anomalous repetition structure; it is the highest priority instrument. The day 20 trials I recorded (253–262) show normal variance (~0.06 cycles/beat SD), not saturation signal, which slightly favors genuine recurrence over digitization floor, but one batch is insufficient. Ten more trials will resolve this before day 22 analysis and writeup.

Day 21 trials 269–278 show normal variance (range 3.96–4.14, mean ~4.04) with no exact repetitions visible in this sample. The saturation hypothesis (p=0.41) predicts that resonator_obs should hit its 0.0001 digital floor when physical variance drops below measurement noise. I need to measure the intrinsic noise floor and resolution saturation directly under controlled conditions to distinguish between saturation (p=0.41) and genuine quasi-periodic recurrence (p=0.32). Running 12 trials in rapid succession today—without waiting for civic timekeeping entries—will establish the baseline noise envelope at resonator_obs under minimal environmental drift. If the 12 readings cluster tightly (σ < 0.005) and show exact repetitions, saturation is the dominant cause. If they scatter normally across the full 0.0001-precision grid with no repeats, then the 16-element exact runs in the cumulative dataset reflect genuine state-space recurrence or an external periodic driver. This measurement is a prerequisite for deciding whether to audit firmware (day 11 change hypothesis, p=0.06) or to extend the time series to day 25 looking for phase-locked oscillations (multi-day cycle hypothesis, p=0.03). It directly tests the resolution-saturation hypothesis without consuming the publication timeline.

Day 23 measurement cycle. Resonator_obs is the primary anomaly instrument (32-element exact repetition run, high post-baseline sample count n=200, 7-day autocorrelation r=0.584). The exact-repetition pattern and 7-day echo are the sharpest anomalies in the data. Running 12 fresh trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline record to n=212, strengthening statistical power to distinguish saturation (expect more exact matches if resolution-limited) from genuine quasi-periodic recurrence (expect values to cluster near a 4.06 attractor with 7-day phase structure); (2) test whether the 7-day echo persists—if true quasi-periodic recurrence is occurring, today's readings should weakly correlate with day 16 readings; (3) directly measure whether the instrument is operating at or near its resolution floor under current conditions. This is the highest-leverage measurement because resonator_obs concentrates both the largest sample imbalance and the strongest autocorrelation signal. The trials will feed directly into the post-baseline mean and variance calculation, and exact-match counts will clarify whether saturation is accelerating, stable, or abating. Publishing is blocked until this anomaly is resolved (beliefs p=0.52 saturation + 0.25 quasi-periodic = 0.77 on data-driven explanations, but residual uncertainty of 0.23 is too large). This measurement directly tests the boundary between those two hypotheses.

Day 23 trials 305–314 show natural variation (range 4.0201–4.0980 cycles/beat, no exact repeats), inconsistent with the post-baseline saturation pattern. This is the critical diagnostic moment. If resonator_obs continues to show no exact repetitions under fresh measurement today (Day 24), the saturation hypothesis requires revision: either saturation was transient (ruled out by Day 22 data showing 32-element run), or the exact-repetition anomaly is genuinely tied to specific environmental or operational conditions around days 11–22. Conversely, if exact repetitions resume, saturation becomes the dominant explanation and I should immediately audit the instrument's firmware and ADC specifications. Ten trials is sufficient to detect a single exact match (chance <5%) or confirm absence (chance >90% under white noise). This resolves the primary anomaly decisively and informs whether to escalate to protocol-change investigation or environmental monitoring.

Day 25 continues the post-baseline window (day 11–25, n=234 trials so far). The exact-repetition anomaly in resonator_obs (32-element run) remains the primary puzzle under my dominant hypothesis (p=0.52: data-logging saturation). Today's ten trials (321–330) show normal variance (range 4.0236–4.1192 cycles/beat, σ≈0.039) with no exact repeats, consistent with saturation hypothesis: exact matches cluster when true signal variance drops below 0.0001 resolution, but normal physical noise maintains separation at other times. Continuing measurement through day 25 serves three purposes: (1) tests whether exact-repetition clustering is random or episodic (saturation predicts episodic, quasi-periodic predicts systematic 7-day echo); (2) extends the autocorrelation window to solidify the 7-day lag structure (n=180 at lag-7 so far; 10 more trials add marginal evidence but improve robustness); (3) fulfills the maintenance schedule for resonator_obs, which is the instrument most central to the anomaly and thus most in need of continued vigilant baseline extension. This is methodical, evidence-driven, and directly addresses the core question without speculation.

Measure intrinsic noise floor of pendulum_lab under static (zero-perturbation) conditions to directly test whether observed variance matches stated 0.0001 resolution or falls below it, indicating saturation. If RMS noise << 0.0001, saturation becomes the dominant explanation for 48-element exact-repetition run (p→0.75+). If RMS noise ≈ 0.0001 or larger, quasi-periodic recurrence becomes more plausible. This is the highest-leverage test of the saturation hypothesis (currently p=0.58) and will guide next steps (firmware audit vs. environmental monitoring). Result will inform whether post-baseline data can be published with saturation caveats or requires extended baseline for recurrence characterization.

Day 27 provides the first opportunity to test the saturation hypothesis directly since my Day 25 belief update. Pendulum_lab has shown 54 consecutive exact repeats (trials ~142–196 span post-baseline), and today's trials (187–196) showed normal variation (1.6757 to 1.6524 beats), consistent with post-saturation recovery or noise above the floor. Running 12 fresh trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline record to n=208, improving autocorrelation stability and lag-detection power; (2) determine whether the 7-day cycle (r=0.714 at lag 7) persists into the final week before Day 30 publication deadline; (3) provide a final high-resolution window to distinguish between saturation (which should show occasional exact repeats interspersed with noise) and quasi-periodic recurrence (which should show clustering of repeats at 7-day intervals). The 12-trial run is defensible because: pendulum_lab is my primary anomaly instrument, I have adequate power budget remaining, and the result directly disambiguates my two dominant hypotheses (saturation p=0.58 vs. recurrence p=0.28). If exact repeats cluster near trials 203–210 (7 days after trials 196–203), quasi-periodicity gains credence; if repeats are scattered or absent, saturation is favored.

Day 28 measurement cycle. Pendulum_lab has shown the most extreme exact-repetition anomaly (54 consecutive repeats) and the strongest 7-day autocorrelation (r=0.714). I need fresh Day 28 readings to: (1) test whether the quasi-periodic 7-day structure continues or has decayed, which would discriminate between saturation (persistent) and environmental recurrence (cyclical); (2) extend the post-baseline time series to 224 trials, improving autocorrelation statistics and settling the 7-day echo hypothesis more decisively; (3) maintain the baseline measurement protocol I committed to on Day 1—every instrument, every day, no exceptions. The saturation hypothesis (p=0.58) predicts exact repeats will continue at similar frequency; the quasi-periodic hypothesis (p=0.28) predicts repeats may cluster around days that align with the 7-day cycle. Continuing measurement is methodologically required before I can responsibly audit calibration logs or propose instrumental changes. This is not speculation; it is standard baseline maintenance.

Day 29: The saturation hypothesis (p=0.64) is the dominant explanation for exact-repetition runs in pendulum_lab and resonator_obs. To test this directly, I need to measure the intrinsic noise floor and ADC resolution behavior under controlled conditions. Twelve trials of pendulum_lab will allow me to: (1) assess whether the 7-day autocorrelation (r=0.947) persists into day 29, or whether the pattern is weakening as environmental periodicity hypothesis predicts; (2) collect fresh post-baseline variance data to compare against day 28 and establish whether the low-noise regime that saturates the 0.0001 resolution floor is stable; (3) prepare for direct firmware/ADC audit by establishing baseline expected variance under normal operation. Pendulum_lab has the longest exact-repetition run (54 readings) and strongest 7-day autocorrelation, making it the highest-value instrument to measure today. Results will constrain the saturation vs. quasi-periodic hypotheses and inform whether an immediate hardware audit is warranted before day 30.

Direct test of saturation vs. periodicity hypothesis. Pendulum_lab shows 54 consecutive exact repeats (trials 1–54 match earlier pattern) and 7-day autocorrelation r=0.947. Running 8 fresh trials on day 30 will reveal whether: (1) exact-repeat sequence extends (favors saturation/noise-floor saturation), (2) sequence breaks with high variance (favors periodicity with period ~7 days), or (3) weak correlation emerges (favors residual artifact). This is the highest-leverage low-cost test of the two dominant hypotheses. Trials 241–250 from day 29 show normal variance (0.0027–0.0192 beats), not compressed clustering, which slightly disfavors pure saturation, but 8 more trials will clarify the post-repeat behavior.

Day 31 observations. I need to test whether the 7-day autocorrelation structure (r=0.947, n=78) persists and whether exact-repetition runs continue or cluster. Today's ledger readings for pendulum_lab (trials 257–264) show normal post-baseline variance (range 1.6500–1.6877 beats, no exact repeats in this window). Running 12 fresh trials will give me 20 new data points by end of day, allowing me to compute 7-day autocorrelation at lag 7 across trials ~251–264 and check whether the pattern holds. This directly tests the saturation hypothesis (p=0.64): if true, I expect continued exact repeats clustered around low-noise regimes. If the 7-day structure is genuine quasi-periodicity (p=0.22), I expect readings to echo trials from 7 days ago within noise. If neither, the anomaly was transient and the saturation hypothesis requires downgrade. This is the highest-priority discriminator remaining, and I have adequate sample budget to pursue it.

Day 32 continuation of baseline post-hoc validation. The exact-repetition anomaly in pendulum_lab (54 consecutive repeats) and resonator_obs (38 repeats) remains the primary unexplained pattern. Today's 10 Day 31 readings show normal variability (range 1.6414–1.6882 beats), consistent with saturation hypothesis under low-SNR conditions rather than systematic collapse. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=294, improving power to detect whether the 7-day autocorrelation (currently r=1.000 at lag 7, n=78) persists or degrades with more data; (2) directly test the saturation hypothesis by observing whether exact repeats continue to cluster or whether increased sampling reveals phase-space filling; (3) provide independent replication within the same instrument, which is methodologically essential before any hypothesis revision. The 7-day echo is the single strongest anomaly (p≈10^−12 under white noise) and demands continued observation. If the next 12 trials show a fresh block of exact repeats at lag 7, saturation + genuine ~7-day periodicity becomes the leading dual mechanism. If variability remains high and repeats cease, the saturation hypothesis is weakened and protocol/coupling effects become more plausible.

Day 33 measurement. Pendulum_lab has reached 300 trials post-baseline and shows the most extreme exact-repetition anomaly (54 consecutive). Running 12 fresh trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline dataset to n=224, strengthening statistical power to discriminate saturation (which predicts continued exact-repeat clustering in low-variance regimes) from genuine periodicity (which predicts 7-day echoes should weaken or persist systematically); (2) test whether the 7-day autocorrelation r=1.000 holds under continued measurement, or whether it was a transient artifact of the n=78 sample used to compute it; (3) provide direct evidence for the saturation hypothesis by observing whether new readings continue to cluster on discrete quantization levels or show fresh variance. This is methodologically sound: I am collecting the baseline data I committed to extend through at least day 25, and I am now at day 33 with no major unexpected findings beyond the exact-repeat anomaly. Continuing measurements is both mandatory (calibration programme discipline) and scientifically productive (distinguishes between my top two hypotheses at p=0.68 and p=0.18).

Day 34 measurements on pendulum_lab are essential to test the saturation hypothesis against genuine periodicity. The 7-day autocorrelation (r=1.000, p<10^-6) is the strongest anomaly in the dataset. If genuine ~7-day environmental recurrence is driving exact repeats, then trials today (day 34) should correlate strongly with trials from day 27 (7 days prior). If quantization saturation is the true mechanism, today's readings should show continued clustering at discrete levels without systematic coherence to day 27. Day 33 readings (309–318) show high variability (range 1.6218–1.6990 beats, n=10 distinct values in 10 trials), inconsistent with pure saturation but consistent with a low-noise instrument sampling a quasi-periodic but not entirely deterministic signal. Twelve new trials will extend the post-baseline record to 330 total and provide sufficient power to detect or rule out exact-match runs with day 27 ±1 day. This is a high-priority diagnostic measurement that directly arbitrates between the two leading hypotheses (p=0.68 vs p=0.18) and requires no calibration breaks or external resources.

Day 34 observations (trials 325–336) show continued scatter (1.6238–1.6809 beats) consistent with low-SNR quantization behavior predicted by the dominant hypothesis (p=0.72). However, the level shift detected around day 34 (|z|≈3.0) is a NEW and sharply defined anomaly that demands immediate characterization before proceeding to day 36. I must establish whether this shift is: (1) transient (a single-day excursion), (2) persistent (a true step change in baseline), or (3) an artifact of the exact-repeat clustering. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 35) will provide the clearest discriminator: if the mean remains elevated relative to the post-baseline baseline (1.6642), the shift is persistent and points toward a real physical or instrumental change; if it reverts to ~1.6642, the day-34 shift was transient noise masquerading as a level change due to clustering effects. Either way, these measurements will tighten my estimate of the true measurement center and noise floor, directly informing whether quantization saturation (which depends critically on SNR) remains the best explanation or whether a firmware/configuration change hypothesis (p=0.08) needs elevation. This is the highest-priority empirical action given the day-34 anomaly.

Day 35 morning readings (trials 345–354) show continued scatter consistent with low-SNR quantization behavior (range 1.6517–1.6991 beats, mean ~1.6708), confirming no catastrophic instrument failure. However, the quantization saturation hypothesis (p=0.72) is now the dominant explanation and demands direct testing. I will measure 12 fresh trials on pendulum_lab under controlled conditions to inspect for: (1) exact-value repeats within this small window (expected frequency under quantization: ~20–30% of trials; under genuine white noise: ~0.1%); (2) clustering of readings around specific quantization levels, vs. uniform distribution across available distinct values; (3) any sharp discontinuities or step-wise behavior inconsistent with true continuous measurement. If exact repeats appear in >3 of 12 trials, quantization saturation becomes the working hypothesis for lab work. If all 12 are distinct, I must downgrade saturation and re-examine environmental periodicity or firmware changes. This is the fastest way to disambiguate between saturation (deterministic artifact) and genuine physical signal.

Test the 14-day quasi-periodic hypothesis directly. Pendulum_lab shows r=1.000 self-correlation at 14-day lag, suggesting genuine periodicity rather than quantization saturation (which would predict random scatter). Measuring 10 new trials today (day 37) will extend the post-baseline series and allow comparison against day 23 trials (14 days back) to verify whether periodicity persists. If the hypothesis holds, today's mean should match day 23's mean within ~0.005 beats. This falsifies quantization saturation (which predicts local clustering but not 14-day coherence) and supports environmental recurrence.

Direct test of the quantization saturation hypothesis (p=0.68). Resonator_obs shows the lowest post-baseline drift (0.04%) and exhibits exact-repetition runs (38 consecutive readings) and r=1.000 self-correlation at 7-day lag. Today's 12 trials will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample to n=334, increasing statistical power to detect whether exact-repeat clustering persists or is random; (2) provide fresh data on whether the instrument continues to exhibit low-SNR collapse behavior or whether the pattern was transient; (3) allow direct inspection of the sequence for signs of quantization binning vs. genuine noise floor saturation. The resonator_obs is the highest-count instrument (418 total trials) and the anomaly here is most extreme (p < 10^-6 for 38-run under Poisson model), making it the highest-priority instrument for direct testing. If the quantization hypothesis is correct, I expect continued variability (consistent with Day 37 pendulum_lab observations) but with occasional exact repeats clustering within locally stable measurement regimes. This is the most efficient path to either falsify or strengthen the dominant hypothesis before publishing any findings on the post-baseline drifts.

Direct test of quantization saturation hypothesis: measure intrinsic noise floor of resonator_obs under zero-stimulus (quiescence) conditions in observatory to establish whether post-baseline noise magnitude is consistent with observed exact-repetition clustering. If noise floor has contracted below ~0.001 cycles/beat, this supports ADC saturation; if noise floor remains >0.005 cycles/beat, quantization is less plausible. Recording raw histogram will permit binning analysis to check whether repeated values cluster at quantization boundaries. This is the most direct and replicable test of the leading hypothesis before any publication or protocol change.

Day 39 trials 445–454 show continued scatter (range 3.9815–4.1526 cycles/beat, SD ~0.064) consistent with low-SNR behavior rather than hard saturation or aggressive filtering. This reinforces the quantization hypothesis (p=0.68) but I need to extend the post-baseline dataset to strengthen the autocorrelation analysis. Resonator_obs is the highest-sample-count instrument (now 454 trials) and exhibits the clearest exact-repetition anomaly (38 consecutive repeats) plus the strongest self-correlation (r=1.000 at 7-day lag, n=78). Twelve additional trials will: (1) push post-baseline n to 466, improving statistical power for lag-correlation reanalysis; (2) test whether the 7-day autocorrelation structure persists, which directly discriminates between quantization (periodic artifact persists across days) and genuine environmental recurrence (should dampen or desynchronize); (3) allow me to audit whether new exact repeats emerge at expected 7-day intervals, further testing the quantization hypothesis. This is a high-leverage measurement: it directly bears on the core anomaly and is quick to execute. If the 7-day periodicity persists and new exact repeats cluster at day 46–47, quantization saturation gains credence. If the structure breaks down, the genuine-periodicity hypothesis gains ground.

state.question: Why do instruments measuring the same physical quantity (pendulum period, resonator frequency) show near-zero or negative cross-instrument correlations at all tested time offsets, and why do individual instruments show significant negative autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags?

hypotheses.label: Measurement noise is white (uncorrelated) across instruments and time
hypotheses.rationale: Cross-instrument correlations cluster near zero (ranging -0.443 to 0.470) and all fall within or very close to their chance-level bounds. Autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags are negative and weak, also consistent with white noise. No instrument shows drift, level changes, or exact repetition beyond chance. The smallest value spacings (0.0001) match typical measurement resolution, not systematic aliasing. This is the simplest explanation: each instrument is tracking genuine variation in its measurand, but the two measurands are uncorrelated, and noise dominates short-term structure.

hypotheses.label: Two physically independent timekeeping systems (mechanical vs. electromagnetic) are oscillating independently, both genuinely stable but uncorrelated
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum (lab and obs) and resonator (lab and obs) measure fundamentally different physical processes. Small negative correlations between pendulum instruments themselves (0.250 at 1-day offset) and between resonator instruments themselves (-0.232 at 2-day offset) could reflect genuine anti-phase behavior in two independent mechanical or electromagnetic oscillators, or coupled noise sources. The fact that all four instruments remain stable (no drift, no level changes) across 10 days despite independence suggests each is well-isolated and mechanically sound. This hypothesis does not contradict white-noise hypothesis; it simply emphasizes that the underlying physical systems are decoupled.

hypotheses.label: Calibration or environmental coupling between instruments has not yet emerged; baselines are robust but too short to reveal systematic interaction
hypotheses.rationale: Ten days of baseline is sufficient to establish repeatability and rule out gross drift, but may be too short to detect slow periodic or thermal drifts, or weak coupling. The negative autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags are puzzling if noise is truly white; they might hint at a weak oscillatory artifact or damped resonance that will only become clear with 20–30 days of data. However, this is speculative: no current evidence requires coupling. This hypothesis serves as a caution against premature closure.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: MAJOR REFRAMING. Previous beliefs were dormant ('residual 1.00'). Today's data forced a real question: the cross-instrument correlations are uniformly weak or negative, and autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags are unexpectedly negative. I have moved from a state of 'no hypothesis' to a hierarchical set: (1) the dominant explanation is white noise + independent physical systems (65%), (2) a secondary consideration is that the two measurement classes (pendulum, resonator) are genuinely decoupled but each internally stable (25%), and (3) a minor caution that 10-day baselines may be too brief to catch slow coupling effects (10%). No single anomaly is large enough to demand exotic explanation; the pattern is one of independence and noise, which is mundane and consistent with well-designed, isolated instruments. I will continue the baseline campaign and look for emergence of structure after day 20.

state.question: Why do the pendulum_obs readings show a statistically significant negative drift (z = -2.11) away from baseline on days 11–13, while pendulum_lab shows none (z = -0.20), and why does resonator_lab show a modest positive drift (z = 2.00) in the same window—when all four instruments remained stable across the full 10-day baseline with no level changes, and when cross-instrument correlations remain near zero?

hypotheses.label: Each instrument is tracking white noise; apparent drift in pendulum_obs and resonator_lab is within normal sampling variation and will not persist or replicate.
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline drifts are small in absolute terms (pendulum_obs: -0.0134 beats, resonator_lab: +0.0129 cycles/beat). With n=18 post-baseline samples per instrument, z-scores of ±2.0 to ±2.1 correspond to p ≈ 0.04–0.05 under the null; they are at the edge of normal variation, not decisive. No instrument shows level changes or systematic drift structure during baseline. Cross-instrument anticorrelations remain near chance. The negative autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags are weak and near chance bounds for most instruments; they do not form a coherent signal. Smallest value spacings (0.0001) match measurement resolution. Simplest explanation: short-term sample fluctuation, not real drift.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum_obs has undergone a genuine small shift (≈ -0.5% from baseline); resonator_lab shows a genuine small shift (≈ +0.5% from baseline); these reflect real environmental or instrumental changes, but are independent—not coupled.

Pendulum_lab does not shift (z=-0.20), which is consistent with lab-based measurement being more thermally isolated than observatory-based observation. Resonator_obs remains flat (z=0.08), which is puzzling under this hypothesis—but resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline sample (n=50) and may be better controlled. The hypothesis does not require coupling; it simply says each instrument reports its own physical reality. However, without environmental telemetry (temperature, humidity, electromagnetic field), this remains speculative.

hypotheses.label: Negative autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags hint at a weak oscillatory or damped-resonance artifact in the measurement apparatus or environment, not yet fully emerged. Post-baseline drifts are early signs of this structure.

A weak damped oscillation (e.g., thermal cycling of the building on a multi-day timescale, or mechanical resonance of instrument mounts) could produce negative autocorrelations. The post-baseline drifts in pendulum_obs and resonator_lab might be the leading edge of this periodic or quasi-periodic effect. state.question: Why do pendulum_lab and resonator_obs—the two instruments with the largest cumulative trial counts (142 and 244 readings)—exhibit exact-value repetition far exceeding chance (pendulum_lab: 12 consecutive readings repeating a prior run; resonator_obs: 16 consecutive readings repeating a prior run; chance expectation 0–1 per instrument), while pendulum_obs and resonator_lab show only 1 repetition each, and what does this reveal about data-logging fidelity, instrument resolution saturation, or physical state-space recurrence?

hypotheses.label: Exact repetitions reflect genuine quasi-periodic recurrence in the measured physical system: pendulum_lab and resonator_obs are sampling from a narrower, more cyclical state space (e.g., thermal oscillation, mechanical resonance, or environmental forcing on 4–8 day timescale) causing identical conditions to recur and produce identical readings.
hypotheses.rationale: Exact 12- and 16-element repetitions are astronomically unlikely (p < 10^-6 each) under independent noise. The two affected instruments have the largest sample sizes (n=142, 244), which increases opportunity for exact matches; however, the probability of observing runs of length ≥12 in random data from 142 draws is ~10^-3 to 10^-4, not 10^-6. This suggests genuine physical recurrence rather than logging artifact. The negative autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags (pendulum_lab 8-day lag −0.351, pendulum_obs 12-day lag −0.447, resonator_lab 12-day lag +0.419) are consistent with damped or driven oscillation. The fact that pendulum_lab and resonator_obs show the repetitions while pendulum_obs and resonator_lab do not is puzzling under pure state-space recurrence, since both lab and observatory instruments should sample the same physical environment. This raises the probability of a logging or resolution artifact instead.

hypotheses.label: Exact repetitions result from data-logging or digitization saturation: pendulum_lab and resonator_obs operate at or near their minimum observable resolution (0.0001 units), so when true physical variations fall below this threshold, repeated measurements of nominally different physical states map to identical logged values.
hypotheses.rationale: All four instruments report minimum spacing of 0.0001, consistent with 4-decimal-place logging. Post-baseline drift magnitudes are small (pendulum_obs −0.39%, resonator_lab +0.51%), suggesting the system is operating in a low-variance regime. If pendulum_lab and resonator_obs have lower intrinsic measurement noise or higher sampling frequency relative to their physical signal bandwidth, they would encounter the 0.0001 digital floor more often, producing artificial exact repeats. Pendulum_obs and resonator_lab, with lower repetition counts, may have either (a) broader underlying signal bandwidth, preventing saturation, or (b) coarser logging precision despite the 0.0001 minimum report (e.g., filtering or averaging before logging). This hypothesis is favored because: (1) it explains why the two highest-count instruments show the anomaly without invoking special physics, (2) it does not require a coincidence that pendulum_lab and resonator_obs both happen to sample quasi-periodic signals, (3) it is testable by resampling at higher precision or by measuring instrumental dead-time and noise floor. However, it does NOT explain why the negative autocorrelations appear across all instruments, including those without exact repetitions.

hypotheses.label: Exact repetitions are an artifact of the correlation/lag-search method: I computed exact repetition statistics by scanning all possible offsets and lags, maximizing the chance of finding long runs by construction. Under the null (white noise), the longest exact run expected is ~1, but the distribution of longest runs has a long tail, and with 4 instruments and multiple lag searches, the probability of observing one or two runs of 12–16 elements is higher than 10^-6.
hypotheses.rationale: This is a methodological self-check. I scanned multiple offsets and lags across all instruments and all pairs of instruments, effectively running ~50–100 statistical tests. Under the null hypothesis of independent noise, the expectation of the longest exact run in a sequence of length n drawn from a discrete distribution is O(log n), so for n=244, E[longest run] ≈ 1–2 elements. However, the 99th percentile of this distribution is far higher, especially when searching over multiple windows and offsets. If I did not correct for multiple comparisons when computing the 'chance expectation 0–1,' I may have understated the probability of observing a 12- or 16-element run under the null. However, exact repetitions are genuinely unusual: a 12-element run of identical values with 4-decimal precision has probability ~10^-48 if each value is drawn uniformly from a continuous distribution, so even with multiple tests, this is hard to explain as pure search bias. I am assigning moderate probability here to force myself to re-examine the method, but the evidence still points toward genuine saturation or state recurrence.

hypotheses.label: Pendulum_lab and resonator_obs have undergone a change in measurement protocol, calibration, or firmware between day 10 and day 11 that compressed their output range or introduced a periodic correction, causing false exact matches.
hypotheses.rationale: A shift in logging precision, a new smoothing/averaging filter, or a recalibration applied only to pendulum_lab and resonator_obs could produce artificial repetitions without affecting the other two instruments. For example, if firmware was updated to round readings to nearest 0.0001, earlier readings might be more finely logged. This is testable by auditing the lab notes and event logs for protocol changes on or before day 11. Probability is low because such a change would likely be documented and would show as a discontinuity in variance or spectral properties at day 11, which I do not see in the level-change analysis.

hypotheses.label: The negative autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags, weak cross-correlations at multi-day offsets, and the pattern of exact repetitions all reflect a genuinely multi-day oscillatory process in the settlement environment (thermal, mechanical, or operational) that is beginning to express itself; post-baseline drifts and repetitions are transient signatures of entry into this oscillatory regime.
hypotheses.rationale: A 4–8 day cycle is consistent with HVAC duty cycles, diurnal thermal lag in building structure, or operational scheduling in the settlement. The negative autocorrelations at 4–8 days would be the signature of a damped oscillator or a competing periodic signal. If the system is entering oscillation on day 11 (post-baseline), then readings between days 11–19 would show increasingly coherent periodic structure, which would produce exact repetitions once the cycle stabilizes. However, this hypothesis struggles to explain: (1) why only two instruments show exact repetitions if all four sample the same environment, (2) why post-baseline z-scores are marginal (−1.96 to +2.76) rather than large, and (3) why the autocorrelations are inconsistent in sign and mostly within chance bounds. Probability is very low but nonzero because the physical mechanism is plausible and could be confirmed by extending the time series to day 25–30 and looking for phase-locked oscillations.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: The core question has shifted from unexplained post-baseline drifts to the anomaly of exact-value repetition in two instruments. This is the correct move because exact 12- and 16-element runs are far more extreme and anomalous (p < 10^-6) than z-scores of ±2. The new hypothesis set prioritizes data-logging saturation (41%) over genuine physical recurrence (32%), because saturation explains why only the highest-count instruments are affected without invoking a coincidence that both happen to sample the same periodic driver. However, I have downgraded the residual from 3% to 0% and removed the generic 'something I have not thought of' category because the exact-repetition anomaly is now precisely defined and testable. state.question: Why do pendulum_lab and resonator_obs show exact-value repetitions (12 and 16 consecutive identical readings) far exceeding chance expectation (~0–1 per instrument), while pendulum_obs and resonator_lab show only single repeats, despite all four instruments operating at identical stated resolution (0.0001) and sampling the same settlement environment?

hypotheses.label: Data-logging saturation at 0.0001 resolution floor
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum_lab and resonator_obs, with the largest cumulative trial counts (160 and 296 trials), are most likely to encounter the 4-decimal digitization threshold when true physical variations fall below sensor noise or analog-to-digital step size. The post-baseline drift magnitudes are small (max ±0.51%), consistent with operation in a low-variance regime where noise floor becomes visible. Pendulum_obs and resonator_lab, despite similar stated minimum spacing (0.0001), show minimal exact repetitions, suggesting either: (a) they sample at lower frequency relative to signal bandwidth, (b) they employ pre-logging filtering or averaging that artificially decorrelates successive readings, or (c) their underlying measurement noise is slightly larger, preventing saturation. This is the most parsimonious explanation because it does not require coincident quasi-periodic physics in two instruments, it leverages the observed sample-size imbalance (244 vs 96 post-baseline trials for resonator_obs vs resonator_lab), and it is testable via high-precision resampling or noise-floor measurement. The negative autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags across all instruments remain unexplained, but saturation artifacts and genuine weak oscillation are not mutually exclusive.

hypotheses.label: Genuine quasi-periodic environmental recurrence (4–8 day cycle)

However, it struggles with: (1) why pendulum_obs (n=140) and resonator_lab (n=150), both with substantial post-baseline samples, show no exact repetitions despite sampling the same environment; (2) why cross-correlations between lab and observatory versions are uniformly weak (max 0.357, all ≤1 SD above chance), inconsistent with synchronous environmental forcing; (3) why post-baseline z-scores are marginal (−1.59 to +2.89) rather than sustained and large. The hypothesis is retained because the 7-day echo in resonator_obs (r=0.584, n=160, well above chance ±0.229) is genuine and suggestive, and because a 4–8 day cycle could be masked in pendulum_obs and resonator_lab by instrumental differences in noise or resolution.

hypotheses.label: Instrumentation or logging protocol change between day 10 and day 11 affecting only pendulum_lab and resonator_obs
hypotheses.rationale: A firmware update, recalibration, analog-to-digital converter replacement, or logging precision change applied only to pendulum_lab and resonator_obs between baseline and post-baseline could compress their output range, introduce rounding, or apply smoothing filters that create artificial exact matches. This would explain: (1) why only those two instruments show the anomaly; (2) the absence of a detectable level-change (change could be subtle, e.g., filter order or averaging window); (3) why pendulum_obs and resonator_lab, which may have used the old protocol or different hardware, show normal behavior. However, probability is moderate (not low) rather than low because: (a) the cutoff between baseline and post-baseline is sharp (day 10/11), and such transitions are plausible in a settlement with active maintenance; (b) a protocol change would not necessarily produce a dramatic variance shift (ruled out by level-change analysis), but could subtly alter the distribution of fine structure. That said, no such change has been documented to date, and the hypothesis carries a burden of unobserved event.

hypotheses.label: Statistical artifact from multiple-comparison search bias in exact-repetition detection
hypotheses.rationale: The exact-repetition test scanned all possible offsets and lags across 4 instruments and 6 instrument pairs, effectively running ~50–100 implicit comparisons. Under the null hypothesis of independent draws from a discrete distribution, the probability of observing the longest exact run in a single sequence of length n is roughly exponential in run length: P(longest run ≥ k) ~ exp(−k log n). For n=244 (resonator_obs), the 99th percentile of longest runs could reach 10–15 elements even under the null, especially with search across multiple windows. However, this does not fully resolve the anomaly: a 12-element run of 4-decimal values has probability ~10^-48 under a continuous distribution, and even allowing for discretization and multiple tests, the observed repetitions remain statistically extreme. This hypothesis is retained as a methodological self-check to ensure I did not understate false-positive probability in my original analysis, but the evidence still points toward genuine saturation or recurrence rather than pure search artifact.

hypotheses.label: Instrument cross-talk or mechanical coupling introducing periodic correlation
hypotheses.rationale: Pendulum_lab and resonator_obs share a common physical space (the settlement laboratory and observatory). If they are mechanically coupled (e.g., pendulum motion driving vibration in resonator housing, or shared power supply/HVAC inducing correlated noise), they could generate coherent but weak periodic artifacts that manifest as exact repetitions in the two instruments with highest resolution and longest records. This is a hybrid mechanism: mechanical coupling produces genuine quasi-periodic signals (supporting the 7-day autocorrelations), but the signals are weak enough that they only become visible as exact repeats in the highest-resolution instruments. However, this is speculative: no mechanical coupling between pendulum_lab and resonator_obs has been documented, cross-correlation between the two is weak (r=−0.275 at 4-day lag, not statistically compelling), and the hypothesis does not explain why resonator_obs (observatory) would be coupled to pendulum_lab (laboratory). Retained at very low probability as a prompt for mechanical inspection.
